65715.m: The World Council of Churches has existed since 1948.

65716.q: Which large church is not a full member of the World Council of Churches?
65716.e: The Roman Catholic Church works closely with the WCC but is not a member. It sends observers and members to some commissions.
65716.m: The Catholic Church works with the World Council of Churches without being a member.

65717.q: When does the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity take place each year?
a: In the first week of Advent
65717.e: In the northern hemisphere the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity is held from 18 to 25 January. Churches of different denominations pray together.
65717.m: In January, Christians pray for their unity for a week.

65718.q: Which ecumenical community in France did the Swiss Brother Roger found?
65718.e: Brother Roger Schutz founded the Taizé Community in Burgundy in 1940. Every year thousands of young people from many denominations go there.
65718.m: Taizé is a meeting place for young people of all denominations.

65719.q: Which two churches reached agreement in Augsburg in 1999 on an old dispute from the time of the Reformation?
65719.e: In 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church signed a joint declaration. This largely settled an important dispute from Luther's time.
65719.m: Catholics and Lutherans found a shared view in 1999.

65720.q: Which two churches withdrew their mutual condemnations from the Middle Ages in 1965?
a: The Catholic and the Orthodox Church
The Reformed and the Lutheran Church
The Anglican and the Methodist Church
The Coptic and the Armenian Church
65720.e: In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the excommunications from the year 1054. That was an important step towards reconciling the Western and Eastern Churches.
65720.m: Since 1965 the old excommunications between Rome and Constantinople have been lifted.

65721.q: What is the ecumenical association of Christian churches in Switzerland called?
a: Council of Christian Churches in Switzerland
65721.e: In the Council of Christian Churches in Switzerland (AGCK), Catholic, Reformed, Christian Catholic, Orthodox and other churches work together. It was founded in 1971.
65721.m: The AGCK connects the churches of Switzerland.

65722.q: Which sacrament may also be validly given by a person who is not ordained in an emergency?
65722.e: When a life is in danger, anyone may carry out an emergency baptism by pouring water over the head and saying the words of baptism.
65722.m: In an emergency, anyone may baptise.

65723.q: How many sacraments does the Catholic Church have?
65723.e: The seven sacraments are baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, ordination and marriage.
65723.m: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments.

65724.q: With which sacrament is a person received into the Church?
65724.e: Baptism is the first sacrament. Through it a person becomes a member of the Church. Confirmation and the Eucharist follow later.
65724.m: You are received into the Church through baptism.

65725.q: How is a sacrament often briefly described?
a: A visible sign of God's invisible grace
A hymn in a church service
65725.e: Augustine already described sacraments as visible signs of an invisible reality, for example water in baptism.
65725.m: A sacrament lets people experience God's closeness through a visible sign.

65726.q: Which sacrament has three levels: deacon, priest and bishop?
65726.e: The sacrament of holy orders is given in three levels: ordination as a deacon, as a priest and as a bishop.
65726.m: Ordination has the levels deacon, priest and bishop.

65727.q: According to Catholic teaching, who gives the sacrament of marriage?
a: The bride and groom to each other
65727.e: In the Latin Church, the bride and groom give the sacrament to each other. The priest or deacon is present as the Church's witness.
65727.m: At a Catholic wedding, the couple give the sacrament to each other.

65728.q: Which three Catholic sacraments can you only receive once in your life?
a: Confirmation, marriage, anointing of the sick
65728.e: According to Catholic teaching, baptism, confirmation and ordination leave an indelible mark and are therefore not repeated.
65728.m: Baptism, confirmation and ordination are received only once.

65729.q: How many sacraments do the Reformed churches have?
65729.e: The reformers only recognised baptism and Holy Communion as sacraments. The Catholic Church, on the other hand, kept seven sacraments.
65729.m: The Reformed churches have two sacraments: baptism and Holy Communion.

65730.q: What does the Greek word ‘mysterion’, which Orthodox Christians use for the sacraments, mean?
65730.e: Mysterion means mystery or secret. That is why the Eastern Churches call the sacraments mysteries.

65731.q: What does the Greek word ‘Eucharist’ mean?
65731.e: Eucharistia means thanksgiving in Greek. At the Last Supper Jesus said the prayer of thanks over the bread and wine.

65732.q: What is the thin, round bread given at Catholic communion called?
65732.e: The host is made of unleavened wheat dough. The name comes from the Latin ‘hostia’, meaning offering.
65732.m: At communion, Catholics receive the host.

65733.q: What is the decorated cabinet in Catholic churches where the consecrated hosts are kept called?
65733.e: The consecrated hosts are kept in the tabernacle, for example for communion for the sick. The word comes from the Latin ‘tabernaculum’, meaning tent.
65733.m: The consecrated hosts are kept in the tabernacle.

65734.q: What does the ‘sanctuary lamp’ in a Catholic church show?
a: There are consecrated hosts in the tabernacle
The service is about to begin
65734.e: The sanctuary lamp, usually red, burns all the time near the tabernacle and shows the presence of Christ in the Eucharistic bread.
65734.m: The sanctuary lamp shows that hosts are kept in the tabernacle.

65735.q: How long should Catholics go without eating before receiving communion?
65735.e: Since 1964 Church law has required a Eucharistic fast of one hour. Water and medicine are allowed.
65735.m: Before communion you fast for one hour.

65736.q: What is the chalice used for at Mass?
65736.e: At Mass the wine is offered in the chalice. The hosts, on the other hand, lie in a bowl or in the ciborium.
65736.m: At Mass the wine is in the chalice.

65737.q: What are Jesus' words ‘This is my body’, spoken at Mass and Holy Communion, called?
65737.e: With the words of institution, the Church remembers how Jesus gave bread and wine at the Last Supper.
65737.m: The words of institution recall the Last Supper.

65738.q: How did Huldrych Zwingli understand Holy Communion?
a: As a memorial meal that remembers Jesus
As a sacrifice needed every day
As a feast only for priests
65738.e: Zwingli read the word ‘is’ as ‘means’: bread and wine are signs that recall Jesus' death.
65738.m: For Zwingli, Holy Communion was above all a meal of remembrance.

65739.q: What could Luther and Zwingli not agree on in 1529?
65739.e: At the Marburg Colloquy, Luther and Zwingli agreed on many points, but not on how to understand the bread and wine in Holy Communion.
65739.m: Luther and Zwingli argued about Holy Communion.

65740.q: In which Zurich church did Huldrych Zwingli preach?
65740.e: Zwingli was pastor at the Grossmünster in Zurich. There, in 1525, Holy Communion was celebrated in Reformed form for the first time.
65740.m: Zwingli preached in the Grossmünster in Zurich.

65741.q: What do the faithful receive at Reformed Holy Communion?
a: Bread and wine or grape juice
65741.e: Reformed congregations share bread and wine. Grape juice is often offered too, so that children and people who do not drink alcohol can take part.
65741.m: At Holy Communion the congregation shares bread and wine or grape juice.

65742.q: What did Martin Luther teach about the bread and wine in Holy Communion?
a: Christ is really present in them
They are only signs without meaning
65742.e: Luther held to the real presence of Christ ‘in, with and under’ the bread and wine, without taking over the Catholic teaching of transformation.
65742.m: Luther believed in the real presence of Christ in Holy Communion.

65743.q: What was important to the reformers at Holy Communion that was hardly usual for lay people in the Middle Ages?
65743.e: In the late Middle Ages lay people usually only received the host. The reformers gave the bread and the cup to all the faithful.
65743.m: The Reformation gave the cup back to all the faithful.

65744.q: What vessels were used to give out Holy Communion in Zurich after the Reformation, to avoid splendour?
65744.e: Zwingli wanted simplicity, so in Zurich plain wooden cups and plates were used instead of golden chalices.
65744.m: Zurich deliberately celebrated Holy Communion with simple wooden vessels.

65745.q: What else is the sacrament of confession called in the Catholic Church today?
65745.e: Confession is also called the sacrament of penance or the sacrament of reconciliation, because it brings reconciliation with God and the Church.
65745.m: Confession is the sacrament of reconciliation.

65746.q: What is the forgiveness of sins at the end of confession called?
65746.e: The priest gives absolution: ‘I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’
65746.m: Absolution is the forgiveness of sins.

65747.q: What does the seal of confession forbid a priest to do?
a: Tell anyone what he has heard
65747.e: The seal of confession is strict: a priest must not reveal to anyone what was entrusted to him in confession.
65747.m: The priest must keep to himself what is said in confession.

65748.q: What is the small room or booth where people usually used to go to confession called?
65748.e: In the confessional, the priest and the person confessing are separated by a grille. Today there are also confession rooms for a conversation.
65748.m: Confession used to take place mostly in the confessional.

65749.q: What is honestly thinking about your own wrongdoings before confession called?
65749.e: Before confession, in the examination of conscience, you think about where you have done wrong to others, to yourself or to God.
65749.m: Before confession you examine your conscience.

65750.q: According to Church law, how often should Catholics go to confession at least?
65750.e: Since the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, there has been a duty to go to confession at least once a year, usually before Easter.
65750.m: Catholics should go to confession at least once a year.

65751.q: According to Catholic teaching, what belongs to confession apart from confessing and absolution?
65751.e: Confession includes remorse, confessing your sins, penance or making amends, and absolution.
65751.m: Without remorse there is no valid confession.

65752.q: Who may give absolution in the Catholic Church?
65752.e: Only ordained priests and bishops may give absolution in the sacrament of penance.
65752.m: Only a priest or bishop gives absolution.

65753.q: What does the Latin word ‘confirmatio’, from which ‘confirmation’ comes, mean?
65753.e: Confirmatio means strengthening or affirming: confirmation strengthens the faith that was given at baptism.

65754.q: Who usually gives the sacrament of confirmation?
a: The bishop or someone he appoints
65754.e: The ordinary minister of confirmation is the bishop. He can appoint a priest, such as an episcopal vicar, to do it.
65754.m: Confirmation is usually given by the bishop.

65755.q: Which oil is used to anoint the forehead at confirmation?
65755.e: Chrism is a blessed oil made of olive oil and balsam. With it, the minister makes a cross on the forehead.
65755.m: At confirmation the forehead is anointed with chrism.

65756.q: Which event in the Bible is confirmation especially linked to?
65756.e: At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down on the disciples. According to Catholic belief, confirmation also gives the Holy Spirit.
65756.m: Confirmation recalls the events of Pentecost.

65757.q: How many ‘gifts of the Holy Spirit’ are traditionally named at confirmation?
65757.e: The seven gifts are wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord.
65757.m: Tradition names seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

65758.q: What is the ceremony in Protestant churches called at which young people confirm their baptism?
65758.e: In Reformed and Lutheran churches, young people affirm their own yes to their baptism at confirmation.

65759.q: What words does the bishop say when anointing at confirmation?
a: ‘Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.’
‘I baptise you in the name of the Father.’
65759.e: With these words the minister makes the sign of the cross with chrism on the forehead of the person being confirmed.
65759.m: The words of confirmation are ‘Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.’

65760.q: Who accompanies a young person being confirmed as a special companion?
65760.e: The confirmation sponsor accompanies the young person on their path of faith and places a hand on their shoulder during the ceremony.
65760.m: A sponsor accompanies the person being confirmed.

65761.q: What was the anointing of the sick usually called in the past?
65761.e: Because for a long time it was mainly given to the dying, it was called extreme unction. The Second Vatican Council stressed the name anointing of the sick.
65761.m: What used to be extreme unction is now called anointing of the sick.

65762.q: What does the priest anoint with in the anointing of the sick?
65762.e: The priest uses the oil of the sick blessed by the bishop. The Letter of James already says that the sick should be anointed with oil.
65762.m: Blessed oil is used in the anointing of the sick.

65763.q: Which parts of the body does the priest anoint in the anointing of the sick?
65763.e: The priest anoints the forehead and the palms of the hands with the blessed oil of the sick and prays for strength.
65763.m: In the anointing of the sick, the forehead and hands are anointed.

65764.q: Who may give the anointing of the sick?
65764.e: According to Catholic Church law, only a priest can validly give the anointing of the sick.
65764.m: The anointing of the sick is given by a priest.

65765.q: Can you receive the anointing of the sick more than once in your life?
a: Yes, for example with a new serious illness
65765.e: The anointing of the sick can be repeated, for example when an illness gets worse or before a serious operation.
65765.m: You can receive the anointing of the sick several times.

65766.q: How many different holy oils does the bishop bless every year at the Chrism Mass?
65766.e: The chrism, the oil of catechumens and the oil of the sick are blessed. The ceremony takes place in Holy Week.
65766.m: Every year the bishop blesses three holy oils.

65767.q: What is the anointing of the sick mainly meant to give a sick person?
a: A long life without a doctor
65767.e: The anointing of the sick does not replace medicine. It is meant to strengthen the sick in faith, comfort them and give them peace.
65767.m: The anointing of the sick aims to strengthen and comfort the sick.

65768.q: What liturgical colour does the priest wear in Advent?
65768.e: Purple is the colour of preparation and reflection. It is worn in Advent and in Lent.
65768.m: In Advent the liturgical colour is purple.

65769.q: Which liturgical colour belongs to Pentecost?
65769.e: Red recalls the fire of the Holy Spirit, who came on the disciples like tongues of fire at Pentecost.
65769.m: At Pentecost the liturgical colour is red.

65770.q: What colour belongs to Ordinary Time, the Sundays without a big feast?
65770.e: Green stands for hope and growth and marks most weeks of the year.
65770.m: In Ordinary Time priests wear green vestments.

65771.q: Which liturgical colour is worn at Christmas and Easter?
65771.e: White or gold stands for joy, light and purity and belongs to the great feasts of Christ.
65771.m: At Christmas and Easter the colour is white.

65772.q: On which two Sundays may rose pink be worn in the Catholic Church?
a: 3rd Sunday of Advent and 4th Sunday of Lent
1st Sunday of Advent and Easter Sunday
65772.e: On Gaudete Sunday in Advent and Laetare Sunday in Lent, joyful expectation shines through: purple is lightened to rose.
65772.m: Rose shows joyful expectation on Gaudete and Laetare.

65773.q: What liturgical colour do priests wear on the feasts of martyrs?
65773.e: Red recalls the blood of the martyrs, who were killed because of their faith.
65773.m: On martyrs' feasts the colour is red.

65774.q: Which liturgical colour is used for Good Friday in the Catholic Church today?
65774.e: Since the liturgical reform after the Second Vatican Council, the priest wears red on Good Friday, the colour of Christ's suffering and blood.
65774.m: On Good Friday the liturgical colour today is red.

65775.q: What is the narrow band in the liturgical colour that priests and deacons wear called?
65775.e: The stole is part of the dress of ordained ministers. The priest wears it around his neck, the deacon diagonally across his shoulder.
65775.m: Priests wear the stole in the colour of the day.

65776.q: What does the church year begin with?
65776.e: The church year begins with the first Sunday of Advent at the end of November or the beginning of December.
65776.m: The church year begins with the 1st Sunday of Advent.

65777.q: What are the three large parts of the Catholic church year?
a: Christmas cycle, Easter cycle, Ordinary Time
65777.e: The church year is divided into the Christmas cycle, the Easter cycle and Ordinary Time.
65777.m: The church year has two festive cycles and Ordinary Time.

65778.q: How is the date of Easter worked out?
a: Sunday after the first full moon of spring
65778.e: By an old church rule, Easter is celebrated on the Sunday after the first full moon in spring. For the Church, spring always begins on 21 March.
65778.m: Easter is on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring.

65779.q: What is the earliest possible date for Easter Sunday?
65779.e: Because the Church fixes the start of spring on 21 March, Easter can be at the earliest on 22 March and at the latest on 25 April.
65779.m: Easter falls on 22 March at the earliest.

65780.q: Counting Easter Sunday, on which day of the Easter season is Pentecost?
65780.e: The word Pentecost comes from the Greek ‘pentekoste’, the fiftieth day. Easter Sunday is counted too.
65780.m: Pentecost is the fiftieth day of the Easter season.

65781.q: Which feast is celebrated on 2 February, 40 days after Christmas?
65781.e: At Candlemas, the feast of the Presentation of the Lord, people remember Jesus being presented in the Temple. Candles are blessed.
65781.m: At Candlemas on 2 February candles are blessed.

65782.q: When does Switzerland celebrate the Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer?
a: On the last Sunday in June
65782.e: The Day of Prayer is a holiday shared by all denominations. The Federal Diet set it on the third Sunday in September in 1832. Only Geneva celebrates its own day of prayer in September.
65782.m: The Day of Prayer is on the third Sunday in September.

65783.q: On which day is the feast of the Annunciation celebrated, nine months before Christmas?
65783.e: On 25 March people remember the angel Gabriel's message to Mary, exactly nine months before 25 December.

65784.q: What does the name of the feast ‘Corpus Christi’ mean?
65784.e: ‘Corpus Christi’ is Latin for ‘Body of Christ’, and the old German name ‘Fronleichnam’ also means ‘Body of the Lord’. The feast celebrates the presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
65784.m: Corpus Christi means Body of the Lord.

65786.q: What do Catholic Christians celebrate at Corpus Christi?
a: That Jesus is present in the bread of the Eucharist
65786.e: The feast celebrates the presence of Christ in the consecrated host. It has existed since the Middle Ages.
65786.m: Corpus Christi celebrates Jesus in the bread of the Eucharist.

65787.q: In what is the host carried through the streets in the Corpus Christi procession?
65787.e: The monstrance is a precious display vessel with a glass window so that everyone can see the consecrated host.
65787.m: At Corpus Christi the monstrance is carried through the streets.

65788.q: Under what kind of portable roof does the priest walk with the monstrance in the Corpus Christi procession?
65788.e: A cloth canopy is held over the monstrance by several bearers as a sign of reverence.
65788.m: The monstrance is carried under a canopy.

65789.q: In which canton is Corpus Christi a public holiday?
65789.e: Corpus Christi is a holiday mainly in cantons with a Catholic tradition, such as Lucerne, Uri or Valais.
65789.m: In Catholic cantons such as Lucerne, Corpus Christi is a day off.

65790.q: What do believers in some villages lay on the streets at Corpus Christi?
65790.e: For the procession, beautiful pictures made of petals are laid on the route, and the monstrance is carried over them.
65790.m: At Corpus Christi, carpets of flowers decorate the procession route.

65791.q: On which date is the Assumption of Mary celebrated?
65791.e: The Assumption of Mary is on 15 August and is one of the most important feasts of Mary.
65791.m: The Assumption of Mary is on 15 August.

65792.q: What do Catholics celebrate at the Assumption of Mary?
a: That Mary was taken up into heaven body and soul
The wedding of Mary and Joseph
65792.e: According to Catholic belief, at the end of her life Mary was taken up into heaven body and soul. The Church celebrates this on 15 August.
65792.m: At the Assumption, people celebrate Mary being taken up into heaven.

65793.q: What is blessed in many Catholic areas at the Assumption of Mary?
65793.e: On 15 August believers bring bunches of healing herbs and flowers to church to be blessed.
65793.m: At the Assumption, herbs are blessed.

65794.q: What is the difference between the Ascension of Christ and the Assumption of Mary?
a: Mary was taken up, Jesus rose up himself
Both are on the same day
65794.e: The Ascension of Christ is called Ascensio in Latin, the Assumption of Mary Assumptio: Mary was taken up by God.
65794.m: Jesus ascended into heaven, Mary was taken up.

65795.q: Which churches celebrate a great feast of Mary on 15 August?
a: The Catholic and the Orthodox Church
65795.e: The Catholic Church celebrates the Assumption of Mary, and on the same day the Orthodox Church celebrates the Dormition of the Mother of God. The Reformed Church has no such feasts of Mary.
65795.m: Catholics and Orthodox Christians celebrate a feast of Mary on 15 August.

65796.q: In which canton is the Assumption of Mary an official public holiday?
65796.e: In Catholic cantons such as Ticino, Valais or Uri, 15 August is a public holiday.
65796.m: In Ticino, 15 August is a public holiday.

65797.q: What is 15 August called in Italy, where it is a big holiday?
65797.e: Ferragosto goes back to an ancient Roman festival in honour of Emperor Augustus. Later the Church placed the feast of Mary's Assumption on this day, and many Italians go on holiday then.
65797.m: In Italy, 15 August is called Ferragosto.

65798.q: On which date is All Souls' Day?
65798.e: All Souls' Day on 2 November comes directly after All Saints' Day and is dedicated to remembering all the dead.
65798.m: All Souls' Day is on 2 November.

65799.q: Who is All Souls' Day dedicated to?
65799.e: While All Saints' Day honours the saints, on All Souls' Day people remember everyone who has died.
65799.m: On All Souls' Day people remember all the dead.

65800.q: Which holiday is All Souls' Day on the day directly after?
65800.e: All Saints' Day is on 1 November, and All Souls' Day follows on 2 November. First the saints are honoured, then all the dead are remembered.
65800.m: All Souls' Day comes directly after All Saints' Day.

65801.q: What do many people place on graves on All Souls' Day?
65801.e: The little lights on the graves are a sign of hope for eternal light for the dead.
65801.m: On All Souls' Day lights burn on the graves.

65802.q: Which liturgical colour is usual on All Souls' Day?
65802.e: To remember the dead, the priest wears purple or black vestments, which stand for mourning and penance.
65802.m: On All Souls' Day the priest wears purple or black.

65803.q: What is the well-known festival in Mexico that is celebrated around All Saints' and All Souls' Day called?
65803.e: On the ‘Day of the Dead’, families in Mexico decorate altars with marigolds, photos and food for their loved ones who have died.
65803.m: Mexico celebrates the Día de los Muertos.

65804.q: Where do many families go together on All Saints' and All Souls' Day?
65804.e: Many families visit the graves of their loved ones, decorate them and light candles. There is often a blessing of the graves too.
65804.m: On All Souls' Day people visit the graves.

65805.q: What idea lies behind praying for the dead on All Souls' Day?
a: The dead come back as ghosts
65805.e: According to Catholic teaching, the living can help the dead on their way to God through prayer and Masses.
65805.m: On All Souls' Day Catholics pray for the dead.

65806.e: Trinity Sunday comes one week after Pentecost, when the Easter season has ended.
65806.m: Trinity Sunday is the Sunday after Pentecost.

a: God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit
65807.e: The feast celebrates belief in one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
65807.m: On Trinity Sunday people celebrate the triune God.

65808.q: What is Trinity Sunday often called in Protestant churches in German-speaking countries?
65808.e: Trinitatis comes from the Latin ‘trinitas’, threeness. The following Sundays are called ‘Sundays after Trinity’.
65808.m: German-speaking Protestants call the Sunday after Pentecost Trinitatis.

65809.q: According to Christian belief, how many persons does God consist of in the Trinity?
65809.e: Christians believe in one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The feast of the Trinity has applied to the whole Church since 1334.
65809.m: The Trinity is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

65810.q: Which geometric shape is a common symbol of the Trinity?
65810.e: The equilateral triangle, often with an eye inside, shows three equal sides that form one unit.
65810.m: The triangle is a symbol of the Trinity.

65811.q: With which plant is Saint Patrick said to have explained the Trinity in Ireland?
65811.e: According to legend, Patrick showed a three-leaved shamrock: three leaves and yet one plant.
65811.m: According to Patrick, the shamrock explains the Trinity.

65812.q: What task does Jesus give the disciples at the end of the Gospel of Matthew?
a: To baptise and teach all nations
65812.e: In the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19), Jesus sends the disciples out to baptise in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
65812.m: The Great Commission names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

a: On the last Sunday before the 1st Sunday of Advent
On the first Sunday in January
65813.e: Eternity Sunday is the last Sunday of the Protestant church year, directly before the 1st Sunday of Advent.
65813.m: Eternity Sunday is the last Sunday of the church year.

65814.q: Who do many people think of especially on Eternity Sunday?
a: Their loved ones who have died
65814.e: On Eternity Sunday Protestant congregations remember the people who have died in the past year. Their names are often read out in the service.
65814.m: On Eternity Sunday people think of the dead.

65815.q: Which other name is commonly used for Eternity Sunday?
65815.e: The name Sunday of the Dead stresses remembrance, the name Eternity Sunday the hope of eternal life.
65815.m: Eternity Sunday is also called Sunday of the Dead.

65816.q: In which churches is Eternity Sunday mainly observed?
65816.e: Eternity Sunday is a Protestant day of remembrance. Catholics remember the dead mainly on All Souls' Day.
65816.m: Eternity Sunday is a Protestant day of remembrance.

65817.q: What do many families visit on Eternity Sunday?
65817.e: Many people go to the cemetery on this day and decorate the graves. They often put a candle or a flower arrangement there.
65817.m: On Eternity Sunday people often visit the graves.

65818.q: In which month is Eternity Sunday?
65818.e: Eternity Sunday is the last Sunday before the 1st Sunday of Advent. That is why it always falls in November, between the 20th and the 26th.
65818.m: Eternity Sunday is always in November.

65819.q: What hope does the name ‘Eternity Sunday’ express?
a: Hope of eternal life with God
65819.e: The name looks beyond death to the Christian hope that the dead are safe with God.
65819.m: Eternity Sunday looks towards eternal life.

65820.q: What do many congregations light for the dead on Eternity Sunday?
65820.e: In many services a candle is lit for each person who has died. The light is a sign of hope.
65820.m: On Eternity Sunday candles are lit for the dead.

65821.q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
65821.e: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre. Only a few hundred people live there.
65821.m: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

65822.q: With which country did the pope sign the treaties in 1929 that made Vatican City a country of its own?
65822.e: In the Lateran Treaty of 1929 the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy reached agreement. Vatican City was recognised as a separate state.
65822.m: Vatican City has been a separate state since 1929.

65823.q: Which currency do people pay with in Vatican City?
65823.e: Because of an agreement with the European Union, the Vatican uses the euro. It even mints its own euro coins.
65823.m: In Vatican City people pay with the euro.

65824.q: In which ancient language does the Holy See in the Vatican publish its most important official documents?
65824.e: Latin is the official language of the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church. In everyday life most people in the Vatican speak Italian.
65824.m: The most important documents of the Holy See are written in Latin.

65825.q: Which city completely surrounds Vatican City?
65825.e: Vatican City is an enclave in the middle of Rome. The pope is also Bishop of Rome.
65825.m: Vatican City lies in the middle of Rome.

65826.q: What does the swearing-in of the Swiss Guard every year on 6 May recall?
a: The battle of 1527, when many guards protected the pope and died
The birthday of the first pope
The building of St Peter's Basilica
65826.e: On 6 May 1527, during the Sack of Rome, the Guard defended the pope and 147 guards died. The swearing-in recalls this day.
65826.m: The Swiss Guard is sworn in on 6 May.

65827.q: What must a Swiss man have completed before joining the Swiss Guard?
65827.e: Guards must be Catholic Swiss men who have completed basic training in the Swiss Army. There are also rules about age and height.
65827.m: A Swiss Guard has done basic military training first.

65828.q: Roughly how many guards does the Swiss Guard in the Vatican have today?
65828.e: In 2018 Pope Francis increased the number to 135 men. Vatican City is very small, so a small guard is enough.
65828.m: The Swiss Guard has up to 135 guards.

65829.q: Who appoints the cardinals in the Catholic Church?
65829.e: The pope appoints new cardinals at a solemn meeting called a consistory. The cardinals advise him and elect his successor after his death or resignation.
65829.m: Cardinals are appointed by the pope.

65830.q: In which room in the Vatican does the conclave take place?
65830.e: The cardinals elect the pope in the Sistine Chapel. The doors are locked during the vote.
65830.m: The conclave takes place in the Sistine Chapel.

65831.q: What colour is the smoke when a new pope has been elected at the conclave?
65831.e: After each vote the ballot papers are burnt. White smoke means a pope has been elected, black smoke means nobody has been elected yet.
65831.m: White smoke shows a new pope.

65832.q: Up to what age may cardinals vote in the conclave?
65832.e: Only cardinals who are not yet 80 when the papal seat becomes vacant may vote. Older cardinals can no longer vote.
65832.m: Only cardinals under 80 elect the pope.

65833.q: What majority does a candidate need to be elected pope at the conclave?
65833.e: A new pope needs the votes of two thirds of the cardinals present. This means he has wide support.
65833.m: A pope needs two thirds of the votes.

65834.q: With which Latin words is a new pope announced from the balcony of St Peter's Basilica?
65834.e: The cardinal protodeacon calls out ‘Habemus Papam’, which means ‘We have a pope’. Then he gives the name of the man elected.

65835.q: Which name did the pope elected in May 2025 choose?
65835.e: On 8 May 2025 the conclave elected Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost. He took the name Leo XIV.
65835.m: Since May 2025 the pope has been called Leo XIV.

65836.q: Which country does Pope Leo XIV, the first pope from this country, come from?
65836.e: Robert Francis Prevost was born in Chicago and was a missionary in Peru for a long time. He is the first pope from the United States.
65836.m: Pope Leo XIV is the first pope from the USA.

65837.q: What rings out in addition to the smoke signal after a successful papal election?
a: The bells of St Peter's Basilica
65837.e: So that the smoke signal is not misunderstood, the bells of St Peter's Basilica also ring after a successful election. That way people in St Peter's Square know for sure.
65837.m: After a papal election the bells of St Peter's ring.

65838.q: In which town is the bishop's seat of the Diocese of Basel?
65838.e: The Bishop of Basel has lived in Solothurn since the 19th century. The cathedral is St Ursus Cathedral.
65838.m: The Bishop of Basel has his seat in Solothurn.

65839.q: Where is the bishop's seat of the Diocese of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg?
65839.e: Despite the long name, the bishop has his seat in Fribourg. His cathedral is St Nicholas Cathedral.
65839.m: The Diocese of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg has its seat in Fribourg.

65840.q: Which diocese covers the canton of Ticino?
65840.e: The Diocese of Lugano covers exactly the area of the canton of Ticino. It is the only Italian-speaking diocese in Switzerland.
65840.m: Ticino forms the Diocese of Lugano.

65841.q: Which diocese does the canton of Valais belong to?
65841.e: The Bishop of Sion is responsible for Valais. In German, Sion is called Sitten.
65841.m: Valais belongs to the Diocese of Sion.

65842.q: Which Swiss diocese, with ten cantons, is the largest by area?
65842.e: The Diocese of Basel includes the cantons of Aargau, Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn and Thurgau, among others. It is the largest diocese in Switzerland.
65842.m: The Diocese of Basel is the largest diocese in Switzerland.

65843.q: Which monastery belongs to no diocese but is led by its abbot like a small diocese?
65843.e: The abbeys of Einsiedeln and Saint-Maurice are territorial abbeys. Like a bishop, their abbot is a member of the bishops' conference.
65843.m: Einsiedeln is not part of any diocese.

65844.q: What is the body in which the Swiss bishops join together called?
65844.e: The Swiss Bishops' Conference has existed since 1863. Its members are the bishops of the six dioceses and the abbots of the two territorial abbeys.
65844.m: The Swiss bishops form the Swiss Bishops' Conference.

65845.q: What is the main church of a diocese, where the bishop has his seat, called?
65845.e: The cathedral contains the cathedra, the bishop's chair. The church gets its name from it.
65845.m: The bishop's church is called a cathedral.

65846.q: In Switzerland, what is the local community of church members, which is often allowed to collect taxes, called?
65846.e: In most cantons the church community is a body under public law. It manages the church, staff and money locally.
65846.m: The church community is the local church body.

65847.q: Who decides on the church community's budget at the church community meeting?
65847.e: At the church community meeting, members vote democratically, for example on the budget and the accounts. It works much like a political municipality.
65847.m: Members have a say at the church community meeting.

65848.q: What is the elected leadership of many Reformed church communities, for example in the canton of Zurich, called?
65848.e: The church board leads the church community together with the pastors. Its members are elected by the church members.
65848.m: The church board leads a Reformed church community.

65849.q: Who elects the pastor in many Swiss church communities?
65849.e: In many cantons in Switzerland, the voters of the church community elect their pastors themselves. This say in decisions is a Swiss speciality.
65849.m: In many church communities the members elect their pastor.

65850.q: What is the unit under Church law of a Catholic community looked after by a parish priest called?
65850.e: The parish is part of the Church's structure with diocese and bishop. The church community, on the other hand, is the body recognised by the state for money and administration.
65850.m: The parish is the Church's community, the church community is the one recognised by the state.

65851.q: In Switzerland, what is the person who looks after the building, bells and order in a church called?
65851.e: The sexton is employed by the church community. Sextons prepare services and look after the church.
65851.m: The sexton looks after the church.

65852.q: What is one reason why church communities often merge today?
a: A ban by the federal government
65852.e: Because many church communities are losing members and money, they merge. In the city of Zurich the Reformed church communities joined together into a single one in 2019.
65852.m: Church communities often merge because of falling membership.

65853.q: Which kind of work is typically offered by a church community?
65853.e: As well as services, church communities offer youth work, work with older people and advice. For this they employ, for example, social deacons.
65853.m: Church communities also offer youth work.

65854.q: Who decides in Switzerland whether and how church taxes are collected?
65854.e: In Switzerland the relationship between church and state is a matter for the cantons. That is why the rules on church tax differ from canton to canton.
65854.m: The cantons decide on church tax.

65855.q: Who has to pay church tax as a private person in Switzerland?
65855.e: Private individuals only pay church tax if they are members of a church recognised by the state. Anyone who leaves no longer has to pay it.
65855.m: Only church members pay church tax.

65856.q: In which canton is church tax voluntary, because church and state have been separate since 1907?
65856.e: Geneva separated church and state in 1907. The churches there depend on voluntary contributions from their members.
65856.m: In Geneva church tax is voluntary.

65857.q: How is church tax worked out in many cantons?
a: As a percentage of the cantonal tax
As a fixed amount per person
By the number of church visits
By the size of the flat
65857.e: The church community sets a tax rate that is applied to the basic cantonal tax. So people who earn more also pay more church tax.
65857.m: Church tax is usually a percentage of the cantonal tax.

65858.q: What is part of the church tax used for?
65858.e: With church tax, church communities pay for pastoral care, buildings and social services. People who are not members also benefit.
65858.m: Church tax also pays for social work.

65859.q: In most German federal states, what percentage of income tax is the church tax?
65859.e: In Germany church tax is 9 per cent of income tax, and 8 per cent in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg. There it is collected by the state.
65859.m: In Germany church tax is usually 9 per cent of income tax.

65860.q: Apart from private individuals, who else pays church tax in most Swiss cantons?
65860.e: In most cantons legal entities such as companies also pay church tax. This money may often only be used for non-religious purposes.
65860.m: Many companies in Switzerland also pay church tax.

65861.q: How does the canton of Vaud fund the recognised churches, even though it has no church tax?
65861.e: In the canton of Vaud the recognised churches are supported from the normal state budget. There is no separate church tax there.
65861.m: Vaud pays for its churches from general taxes.

a: A charity of the Catholic Church
65862.e: Caritas Switzerland helps people in need in Switzerland and abroad. It works with 16 regional Caritas organisations.

65863.q: Who is allowed to shop in a Caritas shop?
65863.e: Caritas shops sell food and everyday products at low prices. Anyone with a shopping card for people on a tight budget may shop there.
65863.m: In Caritas shops, people with little money can shop cheaply.

65864.q: What does the Caritas KulturLegi pass make possible?
65864.e: With the KulturLegi, people on low incomes get discounts on courses, museums, concerts and sport. That way they too can take part in social life.
65864.m: The KulturLegi makes culture and sport cheaper.

65866.q: What does Caritas campaign for especially in Switzerland?
65866.e: Caritas Switzerland and the regional Caritas organisations help people living in poverty in Switzerland. Abroad, Caritas provides emergency aid and development cooperation.

65867.q: What kind of organisation is HEKS?
a: A charity of the Reformed churches
65867.e: HEKS is the charity of the Reformed churches of Switzerland. It helps people in need at home and abroad and is called EPER in French.

65868.q: How does HEKS pay for a large part of its aid projects?
65868.e: Charities such as HEKS depend largely on donations. There are also contributions from the churches and the federal government.

65869.q: Who did HEKS mainly want to help when it was founded?
a: Victims of an earthquake in Japan
65869.e: After the Second World War the Reformed churches founded HEKS as emergency aid for Europe. Later, projects in the global South were added.
65869.m: HEKS first helped people in post-war Europe.

65870.q: In which city does HEKS have its headquarters?
65870.e: HEKS has its headquarters in Zurich. There are also regional offices in several cantons.
65870.m: HEKS has its headquarters in Zurich.

65871.q: Which flowers do volunteers sell before Easter for projects of HEKS and Fastenaktion?
65871.e: In the rose campaign, volunteers sell fair trade roses. The money goes to aid projects of the two charities.
65871.m: Before Easter volunteers sell roses for aid projects.

65872.q: What work does HEKS also do in Switzerland?
65872.e: At home, HEKS works for disadvantaged people. This includes integration projects and legal advice for asylum seekers.
65872.m: In Switzerland HEKS helps asylum seekers, among others.

65873.q: Which topic is one of the main focuses of HEKS's work abroad?
a: The right to land and food
65873.e: HEKS works in more than 30 countries. Important topics are the right to land and food, flight and migration, and climate justice.
65873.m: HEKS works for the right to land and food.

65874.q: What is the joint campaign of HEKS and Fastenaktion in the time before Easter called?
65874.e: The Reformed and Catholic charities run the Ecumenical Campaign together during Lent. It includes, for example, selling roses.
65874.m: The Ecumenical Campaign runs during Lent.

65875.q: What does ‘ordination’ mean in the churches?
65875.e: At ordination a person is solemnly appointed as a pastor or priest. For women people speak of the ordination of women.
65875.m: Ordination is appointment to a church ministry.

65876.q: In which city were the first women in Switzerland ordained as pastors in 1918?
65876.e: Rosa Gutknecht and Elise Pfister were ordained on 27 October 1918 in St Peter's Church in Zurich. They were among the first ordained women theologians in Europe.
65876.m: The first Swiss women pastors were ordained in Zurich in 1918.

65877.q: What reason did the Zurich cantonal government give in 1921 for refusing to let women be elected as pastors?
a: Women did not have the vote
65877.e: The government pointed out that women did not have the right to vote or be elected at that time. So Rosa Gutknecht did not get a permanent post as a pastor and worked as an assistant pastor at the Grossmünster.
65877.m: Without votes for women, women in Zurich could not become pastors for a long time.

65878.q: In which church can women become pastors in Switzerland?
65878.e: Many women work as pastors in the Reformed churches today. This has only been fully allowed in all cantons for a few decades.
65878.m: The Reformed Church has women pastors.

65879.q: Who can become a priest in the Roman Catholic Church to this day?
65879.e: The Catholic Church only ordains men as priests. Pope John Paul II confirmed this in 1994. Many believers would like this to change.
65879.m: To this day, Catholic priests are only men.

65880.q: Which Swiss church that broke away from Rome has also ordained women as priests since 2000?
65880.e: In February 2000 Denise Wyss was ordained in Solothurn as the first woman Christian Catholic priest. The Christian Catholic Church also has no compulsory celibacy.
65880.m: The Christian Catholic Church also ordains women as priests.

65881.q: What does a woman pastor do in a church service?
65881.e: A pastor gives the sermon in the service and explains the Bible. She baptises, marries couples and supports people in difficult times.
65881.m: A pastor preaches in the service.

65882.q: In which churches can women also become bishops today?
65882.e: In some Protestant churches, such as Lutheran ones, women can become bishops. The first Lutheran woman bishop was Maria Jepsen in Hamburg in 1992.
65882.m: Some Protestant churches have women bishops.

65883.q: How do you leave an official cantonal church in Switzerland?
65883.e: Anyone who wants to leave sends a written declaration to the church community or the responsible office. After that, church tax no longer applies either.
65883.m: You leave the church with a written declaration.

65884.q: How many people left the Roman Catholic Church in Switzerland in 2023?
65884.e: In 2023, 67,497 people left the Catholic Church in Switzerland. That was about twice as many as the year before.
65884.m: In 2023 about 67,000 people left the Catholic Church.

65886.q: Which group in Switzerland was larger than the group of Catholics for the first time in 2022?
65886.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, about 34 per cent of the population aged 15 and over had no religion in 2022. Catholics made up about 32 per cent.
65886.m: Since 2022, people with no religion have been the largest group in Switzerland.

65887.q: What financial reason do many people give for leaving the church?
65887.e: Anyone who leaves no longer has to pay church tax. Apart from this reason, many also mention feeling distant from the church or being annoyed by scandals.
65887.m: Many leave to save the church tax.

65888.q: Roughly how many people left the Reformed Church in Switzerland in 2023?
65888.e: In 2023 almost 40,000 people left the Reformed Church. That was about a third more than the year before.
65888.m: In 2023 almost 40,000 people left the Reformed Church.

65889.q: Why are hardly any people recorded as leaving the church in the cantons of Geneva and Vaud?
a: There is no formal membership with church tax
Leaving costs a lot of money
65889.e: In these cantons there is no church tax and no formal membership like elsewhere. That is why hardly any departures are recorded.
65889.m: In Geneva and Vaud hardly any church departures are counted.

65890.q: What share of the Swiss population had no religion around 1970?
65890.e: In 1970 almost everyone in Switzerland belonged to a church, and only about 1 per cent had no religion. Today it is about a third.
65890.m: Around 1970 hardly anyone in Switzerland had no religion.

65891.q: In which country is the village of Taizé with its famous community of brothers?
65891.e: Taizé is in Burgundy, not far from Cluny. Tens of thousands of young people go there every year.

65892.q: Who mainly goes to Taizé to share in community life there for a week?
65892.e: Every year tens of thousands of young people come to Taizé. They pray, sing and talk about their faith.
65892.m: Taizé is a meeting place for young people.

65893.q: What is special about the Taizé Community?
a: Brothers from different denominations live together
65893.e: In Taizé, Protestant and Catholic brothers from many countries live together. The community is a sign of ecumenism and reconciliation.
65893.m: Taizé is an ecumenical community of brothers.

65894.q: How are the well-known songs of Taizé usually built up?
a: Only for organ with no words
65894.e: Taizé songs are made of short verses that are repeated many times. This creates a calm, meditative mood.
65894.m: Taizé songs are short and often repeated.

65895.q: When do the European Youth Meetings of Taizé take place?
65895.e: Since 1978 Taizé has invited young people to a large European city over New Year. The guests usually stay with host families.
65895.m: The European Youth Meetings of Taizé take place over New Year.

65896.q: Where do the guests at Taizé's European Youth Meetings usually stay?
65896.e: The meetings take place in big cities, for example in Basel in 2017/2018. The young people usually stay with families from the region.
65896.m: At Taizé meetings young people stay with host families.

65897.q: Which country did Brother Roger, the founder of Taizé, come from?
65897.e: Brother Roger Schutz was born in 1915 in Provence in the canton of Vaud. In 1940 he founded the community in Taizé in France.
65897.m: The founder of Taizé was Swiss.

65898.q: What are the men who live in the Taizé Community called?
65898.e: The members are called ‘Frères’ in French, meaning brothers. They come from many countries and different churches.

65899.q: Why did the Salvation Army have a hard time in its first years in Switzerland?
a: It met hostility and was partly banned
It was only allowed to sing in English
65899.e: Many people distrusted the new movement, and some cantons banned its meetings. Only in 1889 did the Federal Supreme Court recognise the Salvation Army.
65899.m: At first the Salvation Army met hostility in Switzerland.

65900.q: In which city did the Salvation Army begin in 1865?
65900.e: The founders William and Catherine Booth began their work in the poor East End of London. The movement has been called the Salvation Army since 1878.
65900.m: The Salvation Army began in London in 1865.

65901.q: What do members of the Salvation Army wear at events?
65901.e: The uniform shows that the Salvation Army is organised like an army. The Salvation Army has been active in Switzerland since 1882.

65902.q: What are the local congregations of the Salvation Army called?
65902.e: As in an army, the Salvation Army's congregations are called corps. Their members wear uniforms at events.
65902.m: A Salvation Army congregation is called a corps.

65903.q: What is the well-known Salvation Army motto with three S's?
65903.e: The motto shows that the Salvation Army cares for body and soul. It gives out food, looks after hygiene and spreads the faith.
65903.m: The Salvation Army's motto is ‘Soup, soap and salvation’.

65904.q: Which collection is the Salvation Army known for on Swiss streets during Advent?
65904.e: During Advent, Salvation Army members stand in squares with a kettle and collect money. A brass band often plays as well.
65904.m: With the kettle collection, the Salvation Army raises money in Advent.

65905.q: In which city is the national headquarters of the Salvation Army in Switzerland?
65905.e: Since 1901 Switzerland has been a separate territory of the Salvation Army with its headquarters in Bern. Before that it depended on the headquarters in Paris.
65905.m: The Salvation Army in Switzerland has its headquarters in Bern.

65906.q: Where does the Salvation Army sell donated clothes, books and furniture cheaply?
65906.e: In the Salvation Army's second-hand shops, called ‘Brockis’ in Switzerland, donated things are sold cheaply. The money helps people in need.
65906.m: The Salvation Army runs second-hand shops.

65907.q: Which kind of music is typical of the Salvation Army's services and street performances?
65907.e: The Salvation Army is known for its brass bands. They play in services and on the street.
65907.m: Brass band music belongs to the Salvation Army.

65908.q: On which day is the World Day of Prayer celebrated each year?
a: On the first Friday in March
On the first Sunday of Advent
65908.e: The World Day of Prayer traditionally takes place on the first Friday in March. In 2026 that was 6 March.
65908.m: The World Day of Prayer is on the first Friday in March.

65909.q: Who mainly prepares and leads the World Day of Prayer?
65909.e: The World Day of Prayer is a worldwide movement of Christian women. That is why it is also called the Women's World Day of Prayer.
65909.m: The World Day of Prayer is run by Christian women.

65910.q: What is special about the order of service for the World Day of Prayer?
a: A different country writes it every year
It has been the same for 100 years
65910.e: Every year women from a different country write the liturgy. Then everyone around the world celebrates with this service and gets to know the country.
65910.m: The liturgy of the World Day of Prayer comes from a different country every year.

65911.q: In 2026 women from Nigeria wrote the liturgy for the World Day of Prayer. On which continent is Nigeria?
65911.e: Nigeria is in West Africa and is the African country with the most people. The motto in 2026 was ‘Come! Bring your burdens’.
65911.m: The World Day of Prayer 2026 came from Nigeria in Africa.

65912.q: In which country did the movement that led to the World Day of Prayer begin?
65912.e: In 1887 Christian women met in the USA for a day of prayer. The worldwide movement grew out of this.
65912.m: The World Day of Prayer has its roots in the USA.

65913.q: Roughly how many countries celebrate the World Day of Prayer today?
65913.e: The World Day of Prayer has been celebrated internationally since 1927. Today women in more than 120 countries take part.
65913.m: The World Day of Prayer is celebrated in more than 120 countries.

65914.q: Why is the World Day of Prayer considered ecumenical?
a: Women of different denominations celebrate together
It only takes place in Catholic churches
It is only celebrated by Reformed Christians
65914.e: Catholic, Reformed, Christian Catholic and free church women plan the day together. Ecumenism means the cooperation of the denominations.
65914.m: On the World Day of Prayer, women of different denominations celebrate together.

65915.q: What is the collection on the World Day of Prayer usually used for?
a: For projects for women and girls
65915.e: The money collected supports projects that strengthen women and girls around the world. In this way prayer and action go together.
65915.m: The World Day of Prayer collection supports women and girls.

65916.q: In 2025 the World Day of Prayer liturgy came from the Cook Islands. In which ocean are they?
65916.e: The Cook Islands are in the South Pacific between New Zealand and Hawaii. Women from there prepared the World Day of Prayer in 2025.
65916.m: The World Day of Prayer 2025 came from the Cook Islands in the Pacific.

65917.q: Which pope is Gregorian chant named after?
65917.e: The chant was named after Pope Gregory I, called the Great, who lived around 600. It is not certain whether he collected chants himself, but tradition links his name with this church music.
65917.m: Gregorian chant is named after Pope Gregory the Great.

65918.q: In which language is Gregorian chant traditionally sung?
65918.e: Gregorian chant is the music of the Latin liturgy of the Roman Catholic Church. Its texts mostly come from the Bible, especially the Psalms.

a: In four parts with organ accompaniment
In two parts with a lute
In many parts with an orchestra
65919.e: In Gregorian chant everyone sings the same melody, in unison. Originally it had no instrumental accompaniment.
65919.m: Gregorian chant is singing in unison without instruments.

65920.q: What are the early signs used in the Middle Ages to write down the melodies of chant called?
65920.e: Neumes are signs above the text that show whether the melody goes up or down. Our modern musical notation later developed from them.
65920.m: Neumes are the early notes of Gregorian chant.

65921.q: In which Swiss abbey library is the Cantatorium, one of the oldest surviving chant manuscripts with neumes, kept?
65921.e: The Cantatorium (Codex 359) from the early 10th century belongs to the Abbey Library of St Gallen. The notation used in it is called ‘St Gallen neumes’.
65921.m: The Abbey Library of St Gallen keeps very old chant manuscripts.

65922.q: Who mainly sang Gregorian chant in the Middle Ages?
65922.e: In monasteries people prayed and sang several times a day, in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass. That is why monks and nuns especially cared for chant.
65922.m: Gregorian chant was part of daily prayer in monasteries.

65923.q: On how many staff lines is Gregorian chant usually written in square notation?
65923.e: The square notation of chant uses a staff with four lines. Modern notation, on the other hand, has five lines.
65923.m: Chant notes are usually written on four lines instead of five.

65924.q: What are the scales that Gregorian chant uses called?
65924.e: Chant melodies are in the so-called church modes. They sound different from our modern major and minor keys.
65924.m: Gregorian chant uses the church modes.

65925.q: Where do most of the texts of Gregorian chant come from?
a: From the Bible, especially the Psalms
65925.e: The monks mainly sang psalms and other Bible texts. They decorated their prayer with the melodies of chant.
65925.m: Gregorian chant mostly sings Bible texts.

65926.q: Who composed the St Matthew Passion?
65926.e: Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the St Matthew Passion as cantor of St Thomas in Leipzig. It is regarded as one of the greatest works of church music.
65926.m: The St Matthew Passion is a work by Johann Sebastian Bach.

65927.q: In which church was the St Matthew Passion first performed in 1727?
a: Church of Our Lady in Dresden
65927.e: The first performance took place in 1727 in St Thomas Church in Leipzig. There Bach was responsible for the church music as cantor.
65927.m: The St Matthew Passion was first heard in St Thomas Church in Leipzig.

65928.q: What does the St Matthew Passion tell of?
a: The suffering and death of Jesus
65928.e: A Passion sets to music the story of Jesus' suffering up to his death on the cross. For this Bach used chapters 26 and 27 of the Gospel of Matthew.
65928.m: A Passion tells of the suffering and death of Jesus.

65929.q: Which voice sings the part of the Evangelist, who tells the story, in the St Matthew Passion?
65929.e: The Evangelist is a tenor and narrates the Bible text. The words of Jesus, on the other hand, are sung by a bass.
65929.m: In the St Matthew Passion a tenor tells the story as the Evangelist.

65930.q: What is special about the forces needed for the St Matthew Passion?
65930.e: Bach divided the musicians into two choirs and two orchestras. That way the groups can answer each other as in a conversation.
65930.m: The St Matthew Passion is written for two choirs and two orchestras.

65931.q: What happened to the St Matthew Passion for a long time after Bach's death?
a: It was only played in America
65931.e: After Bach's death the St Matthew Passion was hardly played for about 80 years. Only in 1829 did the young Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy perform it again in Berlin.
65931.m: The St Matthew Passion was almost forgotten for a long time.

65932.q: Which chorale by Paul Gerhardt is heard several times in the St Matthew Passion?
65932.e: This Passion chorale appears five times in the St Matthew Passion with different verses. It runs like a thread through the work.
65932.m: ‘O Sacred Head, Now Wounded’ is the most important chorale of the St Matthew Passion.

65933.q: On which holy day was the St Matthew Passion first performed?
65933.e: Passions were performed in the Good Friday service, the day on which Christians remember Jesus' death. The first performance was on 11 April 1727.
65933.m: Passion music traditionally belongs to Good Friday.

65934.e: George Frideric Handel came from Halle and lived in London for a long time. There he composed his most famous oratorio in 1741.

65935.q: In which city was Handel's ‘Messiah’ first performed in 1742?
65935.e: The first performance took place on 13 April 1742 in Dublin. The work was only played in London for the first time in 1743.
65935.m: Handel's ‘Messiah’ was first heard in Dublin.

65936.q: In which language is the text of Handel's ‘Messiah’ written?
65936.e: Charles Jennens put the text together from the English King James Bible. That is why the work is sung in English.

65937.q: In which city was Handel living when he composed ‘Messiah’?
65937.e: Handel came from Halle in Germany but lived in London for many years. There he wrote ‘Messiah’ in 1741.

65938.q: What tradition is there, especially in Britain, during the Hallelujah Chorus?
65938.e: During the Hallelujah the audience traditionally rises from their seats. Legend says King George II stood up, but there is no proof of this.
65938.m: During the Hallelujah Chorus the audience often stands up.

65939.q: Roughly how long did Handel take to compose ‘Messiah’?
65939.e: Handel wrote the work from 22 August to 14 September 1741. That is only about three and a half weeks for more than 50 movements.
65939.m: Handel composed ‘Messiah’ in just over three weeks.

65940.q: What is an oratorio such as Handel's ‘Messiah’?
a: A work for choir, soloists and orchestra without acting on stage
A play with costumes and scenery
A dance piece for a ballet company
A piece of music only for organ
65940.e: An oratorio is performed like a concert, usually with a religious text. Unlike opera, there are no costumes and no action on stage.
65940.m: An oratorio is a large work for voices and orchestra without acting on stage.

65941.q: At which time of year is Handel's ‘Messiah’ performed especially often today?
65941.e: ‘Messiah’ tells the story from the announcement and birth of Jesus to the resurrection. That is why it is sung especially often in Advent and at Christmas.
65941.m: ‘Messiah’ is often heard at Christmas time.

a: In African American churches in the USA
65942.e: Gospel developed at the beginning of the 20th century in the churches of the African American population in the USA. It combines Christian texts with elements of blues and jazz.
65942.m: Gospel comes from African American churches in the USA.

65943.q: What does the English word ‘gospel’ mean?
65943.e: ‘Gospel’ means the good news, the message of the Gospels. The songs tell of Jesus and the hope of faith.

a: Enslaved African Americans in the USA
65944.e: Spirituals came about in the 18th and 19th centuries among enslaved people of African origin. In Bible stories they found comfort and hope of freedom.
65944.m: Spirituals are the religious songs of enslaved African Americans.

65945.q: Which spiritual tells of Moses and the call ‘Let my people go’?
65945.e: In ‘Go Down Moses’, Moses tells Pharaoh to set the people of Israel free. The slaves linked this story with their own wish for freedom.
65945.m: ‘Go Down Moses’ links the freeing of Israel with the dream of freedom.

65946.q: Which singer was called the ‘Queen of Gospel’?
65946.e: Mahalia Jackson was one of the best-known gospel singers of the 20th century. She also sang at the great March on Washington in 1963.
65946.m: Mahalia Jackson is seen as the Queen of Gospel.

65947.q: What do gospel choirs often do while singing?
a: They clap and move to the beat
They sing with their mouths closed
65947.e: Gospel is lively music. The singers clap, sway to the beat and sing with great joy.
65947.m: Gospel choirs sing in a lively way and clap along.

65948.q: Which way of singing is typical of gospel and spirituals?
a: Call and response between lead singer and choir
A round without words in four groups
Yodelling with quick changes of voice
Speech-song with no melody at all
65948.e: One person sings a line first, and the choir or congregation answers. This form is called ‘call and response’.
65948.m: In gospel the choir answers the lead singer.

65949.q: Which gospel song became a worldwide hit in 1969 through the Edwin Hawkins Singers?
65949.e: The recording by the Edwin Hawkins Singers became a hit in 1969 and entered the charts in many countries. The song is still sung by many choirs today.
65949.m: ‘Oh Happy Day’ is one of the best-known gospel songs.

65950.e: The Sistine Chapel is part of the Apostolic Palace in the Vatican. Today it is part of the Vatican Museums.
65950.m: The Sistine Chapel is in the Vatican.

65951.q: Who is the Sistine Chapel named after?
65951.e: Pope Sixtus IV had the chapel built from 1475. That is why it bears his name.
65951.m: The Sistine Chapel is named after Pope Sixtus IV.

65952.q: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
65952.e: Michelangelo Buonarroti painted the huge ceiling with scenes from the Bible. In fact, he saw himself mainly as a sculptor.
65952.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

65953.q: In which years did Michelangelo paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
65953.e: Michelangelo worked on the ceiling from 1508 to 1512, often on high scaffolding. That was the time of the High Renaissance.
65953.m: The ceiling frescoes were painted from 1508 to 1512.

65954.q: What is the famous ceiling painting in which God gives life to the first human with an outstretched finger called?
65954.e: The fingertips of God and Adam almost touch. This picture is one of the best-known paintings in the world.
65954.m: ‘The Creation of Adam’ shows two fingers that almost touch.

65955.q: Which huge fresco did Michelangelo paint on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel from 1536 to 1541?
65955.e: On the altar wall Michelangelo shows the end of the world with Christ as judge. The picture covers the whole wall behind the altar.
65955.m: On the altar wall Michelangelo painted the Last Judgement.

65956.q: Which technique did Michelangelo use to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
65956.e: In fresco the paint is applied to lime plaster while it is still wet and bonds with the wall as it dries. That is why Michelangelo had to finish one section every day.
65956.m: A fresco is painted on fresh, wet plaster.

65957.q: Which important meeting takes place in the Sistine Chapel?
a: The conclave to elect the pope
The meeting of the Swiss bishops
65957.e: When a new pope is elected, the cardinals gather in the Sistine Chapel. White smoke from the chimney shows that the election has succeeded.
65957.m: In the Sistine Chapel the cardinals elect the pope.

65958.q: Which book of the Bible do the nine main pictures in the middle of the Sistine Chapel ceiling come from?
65958.e: The nine central pictures show stories from the beginning of the Bible, such as the creation of the world and the story of Noah. They all come from the first book of Moses, Genesis.
65958.m: The middle of the Sistine ceiling tells stories from Genesis.

65959.q: Which artist painted the famous wall painting ‘The Last Supper’ in a monastery in Milan?
65959.e: Leonardo da Vinci painted the picture for Duke Ludovico Sforza. It is one of the best-known works of the Renaissance.
65959.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted ‘The Last Supper’.

65960.q: In what kind of room is Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’?
a: In the dining hall of a monastery
In the throne room of a palace
In the crypt of a cathedral
In the kitchen of a castle
65960.e: The picture is painted on the wall of the refectory, the dining hall, of the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie. So the monks ate, as it were, with Jesus and the disciples.
65960.m: Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’ decorates a monastery dining hall.

65961.q: Which moment does Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’ show?
a: Jesus says that one of them will betray him
Jesus is born in the stable
Jesus is baptised in the Jordan
65961.e: Leonardo painted the moment when Jesus announces that one of the disciples will betray him. The disciples react with shock and excitement.
65961.m: The picture shows the excitement after the betrayal is announced.

65962.q: How many apostles sit at the table with Jesus in Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’?
65962.e: Jesus sits in the middle, with six apostles on each side. Leonardo arranged them in four groups of three.
65962.m: In the picture twelve apostles sit at the table with Jesus.

65963.q: Why was Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’ damaged soon after it was made?
a: He painted with tempera on the dry wall
It hung unprotected outdoors for years
It was painted on thin paper
It was drawn in chalk on wood
65963.e: Leonardo did not paint a fresco in wet plaster but experimented with paint on dry plaster. The paint did not stick well and flaked off.
65963.m: Leonardo's new technique made ‘The Last Supper’ fragile.

65964.q: Roughly in which years was Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’ painted?
65964.e: Leonardo worked on the wall painting from about 1494 to 1498. That was during the Renaissance.
65964.m: ‘The Last Supper’ was painted at the end of the 15th century.

65965.q: How can you recognise Judas in Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’?
a: He is holding a money bag
He is wearing a golden crown
He is holding a large key
He is the only one standing up
65965.e: Judas clutches a small bag that recalls the silver coins paid for the betrayal. His face is also in shadow.
65965.m: In the picture the money bag gives Judas away.

65966.q: Which point do the lines of the central perspective in Leonardo's ‘Last Supper’ lead to?
a: The table at the front right
65966.e: All the vanishing lines of the ceiling and walls meet at Jesus' head. In this way Leonardo leads the viewer's eye right to the centre.
65966.m: The perspective leads the eye to Jesus' head.

65967.q: In which city is the Fraumünster with its famous Chagall windows?
65967.e: The Fraumünster stands on the left bank of the Limmat in Zurich's old town. Every year many people visit its colourful choir windows.
65967.m: The Fraumünster with the Chagall windows is in Zurich.

65968.q: Which artist made the stained glass windows in the choir of the Fraumünster?
65968.e: Marc Chagall designed the choir windows as an old man, and they were finished and installed in 1970. They show stories from the Bible in bright colours.
65968.m: Marc Chagall designed the choir windows of the Fraumünster.

65969.q: How many Chagall windows are there in the choir of the Fraumünster?
65969.e: There are five tall windows in the choir, each with its own main colour. In 1978 a rose window in the south transept was added.
65969.m: Five Chagall windows glow in the choir of the Fraumünster.

65970.q: What are Chagall's windows in the Fraumünster especially famous for?
65970.e: Each of the five choir windows has its own main colour, such as green, red, yellow or blue. When the sun shines, the whole room glows with colour.
65970.m: Chagall's windows in the Fraumünster glow in strong colours.

65971.q: Marc Chagall came from a family of which religion?
65971.e: Chagall was born in 1887 in Vitebsk, in today's Belarus, into a Jewish family. In his windows he combines images from the Hebrew Bible with the Christian message.
65971.m: Marc Chagall was a Jewish artist.

65972.q: Who used to live in the convent at the Fraumünster?
65972.e: King Louis the German founded a convent for women in 853 and gave it to his daughter Hildegard. That is where the name Fraumünster, ‘women's minster’, comes from.
65972.m: The Fraumünster used to be a convent for women.

65973.q: What was the name of the last abbess, who handed the convent over to the city of Zurich during the Reformation in 1524?
65973.e: Katharina von Zimmern handed the convent over to the Zurich council voluntarily on 30 November 1524. So the change during the Reformation was peaceful.
65973.m: Katharina von Zimmern was the last abbess of the Fraumünster.

65974.q: On which river is the Fraumünster?
65974.e: The Fraumünster stands on the left bank of the Limmat, opposite the Grossmünster. Both churches shape the look of Zurich's old town.
65974.m: The Fraumünster stands on the Limmat.

65975.q: What is the famous speech that Martin Luther King gave in 1963 called?
65975.e: In the speech King described his dream of a country where all people are treated equally. It is one of the most famous speeches in history.
65975.m: ‘I Have a Dream’ is Martin Luther King's most famous speech.

65976.q: Where did Martin Luther King give his famous speech to about 250,000 people in 1963?
a: In front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington
In Times Square in New York
In front of the Capitol in Atlanta
65976.e: The speech took place on 28 August 1963 during the March on Washington. King spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.
65976.m: In 1963 King spoke in front of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington.

65977.q: Which protest began in 1955 after Rosa Parks was arrested?
65977.e: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger. After that, many African Americans boycotted the buses for more than a year, led by Martin Luther King.
65977.m: The Montgomery bus boycott made Martin Luther King famous.

65978.q: What method did Martin Luther King use in the fight for civil rights?
65978.e: King relied on peaceful protests such as marches, boycotts and sit-ins. He rejected violence because of his Christian beliefs.
65978.m: Martin Luther King fought for equal rights without violence.

65979.q: Which man from India was an important role model for Martin Luther King?
65979.e: Mahatma Gandhi had led India to independence through non-violent resistance. King travelled to India in 1959 to learn more about Gandhi's ideas.
65979.m: Gandhi was a role model for Martin Luther King.

65980.q: Which award did Martin Luther King receive in 1964?
65980.e: In 1964, at the age of 35, King received the Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent fight against racial segregation. At the time he was the youngest winner.
65980.m: Martin Luther King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

65981.q: In which year was Martin Luther King murdered in Memphis?
65981.e: Martin Luther King was shot dead in Memphis on 4 April 1968. He was only 39 years old.
65981.m: Martin Luther King was murdered in 1968.

65982.q: When is Martin Luther King Day in the USA?
a: On the third Monday in January
On the fourth Thursday in November
On the first Monday in September
65982.e: The holiday is close to his birthday on 15 January. It has been observed in the USA since 1986.
65982.m: Martin Luther King Day is on the third Monday in January.

65983.q: In which Indian city did Mother Teresa found her religious order in 1950?
65983.e: Mother Teresa lived and worked in Calcutta, today Kolkata. There she cared for the poorest people in the slums.
65983.m: Mother Teresa worked mainly in Calcutta.

65984.e: Mother Teresa was born in 1910 in Skopje, today the capital of North Macedonia. Only later did she move to India.
65984.m: Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in south-eastern Europe.

65985.q: What is the order that Mother Teresa founded called?
65985.e: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity. The sisters help the poor, the sick and the dying all over the world.
65985.m: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity.

65986.q: What clothing do Mother Teresa and her sisters wear?
a: A white sari with blue stripes
A black habit with a veil
A brown cloak with a hood
A red cape with a belt
65986.e: Mother Teresa chose the simple white sari worn by poor women in India. The blue stripes along the edge are the sign of her order.
65986.m: The white sari with blue stripes is the mark of the sisters.

65987.q: In which year did Mother Teresa receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
65987.e: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her work with the poorest. She asked for the money for the banquet to be given to the poor.
65987.m: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.

65988.q: Which pope declared Mother Teresa a saint in 2016?
65988.e: Pope Francis declared her a saint in Rome on 4 September 2016. She had already been beatified by John Paul II in 2003.
65988.m: Pope Francis made Mother Teresa a saint.

65989.q: Which people did Mother Teresa's family come from?
65989.e: Mother Teresa came from a Catholic Albanian family. Later she became an Indian citizen.

65990.q: What did Mother Teresa work as for many years in India before she founded her own order?
65990.e: As a Loreto sister she taught at a girls' school for almost 20 years. Then she left the school to live directly among the poor.
65990.m: Mother Teresa was first a teacher at a school.

65991.q: Which denomination did Dietrich Bonhoeffer belong to as a theologian?
65991.e: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Protestant pastor and theologian. He taught at the University of Berlin and trained young pastors.
65991.m: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Protestant theologian.

65992.e: Bonhoeffer rejected National Socialism from the very beginning. He was in contact with men who wanted to overthrow Hitler.

65993.q: Which well-known poem did Dietrich Bonhoeffer write in prison at the end of 1944?
65993.e: Bonhoeffer sent the poem to his family as a Christmas greeting in December 1944. Today it is sung as a hymn in many churches.
65993.m: Bonhoeffer wrote ‘By Gracious Powers’ in prison.

a: Shortly before the end of the Second World War
Shortly before the First World War
After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
65994.e: Bonhoeffer was executed on 9 April 1945 in Flossenbürg concentration camp, a few weeks before the end of the war. He was 39 years old.
65994.m: Bonhoeffer was murdered shortly before the end of the war in 1945.

65995.q: Which movement, which fought the influence of the Nazis in the Church, did Bonhoeffer belong to?
65995.e: The Confessing Church opposed the ‘German Christians’, who wanted to adapt the Church to Nazi ideology. Bonhoeffer ran a seminary for preachers for it in Finkenwalde.
65995.m: Bonhoeffer belonged to the Confessing Church.

65996.q: What does Bonhoeffer mean by ‘discipleship’, the subject of a book he wrote in 1937?
a: Inheriting an office from your father
65996.e: In ‘The Cost of Discipleship’ Bonhoeffer explains what it means to follow Jesus seriously. He warns against ‘cheap grace’ without deeds.
65996.m: Discipleship means living by the example of Jesus.

65997.q: In which US city did Bonhoeffer study in 1930 and 1931, going to African American services in Harlem?
65997.e: Bonhoeffer studied at Union Theological Seminary in New York. At the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem he got to know spirituals and the experiences of the Black community.
65997.m: In New York Bonhoeffer got to know African American churches.

65998.q: In which country was Dietrich Bonhoeffer born in 1906?
65998.e: Bonhoeffer was born in Breslau, which belonged to Germany at that time. Later he grew up in Berlin.

65999.q: Where in Africa did Albert Schweitzer found a hospital in 1913?
65999.e: Albert Schweitzer built up a jungle hospital in Lambaréné. There, together with his wife Helene, he treated many sick people.
65999.m: Albert Schweitzer's hospital was in Lambaréné.

66000.q: Which guiding idea is at the centre of Albert Schweitzer's thinking?
66000.e: Schweitzer believed that every life should be respected and protected, that of people, animals and plants. He called this idea ‘reverence for life’.
66000.m: Schweitzer taught reverence for all life.
